results.title: long-term dependencies. Including this and our new perspective, we highlight two critical issues of high recency bias. The first is that a recommendation system with high recency bias seriously lacks serendipity, which is one of the major requirements a fine recommendation system ought to satisfy, as it repeatedly suggests items similar to only those the user recently interacted with. This monotony can quickly bore out user, and further lead to user disengagement. Second, high recency bias means the recommendation system fails to model the entire session into mining user preference, which was the primary goal of sequential recommendation system, and pigeonhole into only users most recent interests, as mentioned in [21]. Still, we lack an universal method to measure this recency bias in existing sequential recommendation models. [21] does measure recency bias, but this is only demonstrated in a reinforcement based setting, not universally applicable to many existing sequential recommendation models, also resulting in the absence of measurement experimental results of recency bias of existing models.

item.text: {"text":"Recent work distinguishes useful recency from excessive dependence on recent events. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) introduces a diagnostic metric and reports accuracy improvements after mitigating measured bias across its evaluated models; this does not establish that suppressing recency always helps. [Spotify’s 2026 benchmark study](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) finds history-aware pairwise transition models outperform SASRec and eSASRec on four of five benchmarks. Older interactions contribute useful evidence even without joint sequence modeling. These datasets differ from the four target categories, so the findings motivate controls rather than predict gains.\n\nFor the proposed diagnosis, these findings support separating history content, order, and branch contributions. On chronological holdouts drawn exclusively from training histories, compare unchanged inputs with repeated order shuffles that preserve the latest item; recent-only versus equally sized older-history windows; and recent-pooling branch ablation while preserving SASRec’s input. Keep targets, candidates, padding conventions, and model weights fixed; report paired target-rank changes and HR@10 changes per category, alongside the macro average. Distinguish repeated-item targets from unseen-item targets to identify whether recent-interest effects concentrate on repetition. These are proposed probes, not a validated intervention recipe: shuffle sensitivity alone cannot establish shortcut learning, and truncation gains may reflect reduced noise rather than preference drift. Select changes using unchanged-input validation performance; use perturbations to localize dependence and failure modes."}
